tools.name: ShowOnboardingRolePicker
tools.description:
Render a clickable role-picker chip row during Cowork onboarding. Call this when asking the user what kind of work they do so they can pick their role and get a matching plugin installed. The role list is hardcoded in the frontend — call with no args.

The call blocks until the user responds. Three resolution paths all land in the tool result: chip click or free-form typed answer → {"role": "Legal"} or {"role": "paralegal"}; X button → {"dismissed": true}. An empty object {} means the user approved without picking a role — treat it like a dismissal. Free-form roles may not match the chip list — search the marketplace with whatever string you get.

Do NOT call this in normal conversation. Only call this when explicitly helping the user set up Cowork for their role/job function.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:

    94	
    95	**`Number` declares nothing (P-165).** Each of the eight number types, and `IntLiteral`, declares its own `asFloat` into `RR64`. So generic code over `T extends Number` can call on a `T` no method or operator that the number types declare, `asFloat` among them. Two numbers of different types compare by `=` only where a coercion carries one into the other: the library declares `=` for each such pair, so a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` of equal value are `=`. Otherwise `=` is `SEQV` ("Traits and objects"), and answers `false` without an error, as for a `ZZ64` against an equal `RR64`. To compare values across types at known types, write `asFloat(x) = y`. In generic code over `T extends Number`, declare your function once for each number type instead. A program may also declare its own number type below `Number` (P-160).
    96	
    97	**An integer power answers its base's type (P-153).** In the interpreter's library, `^` takes an exponent of any integer type. At a negative exponent, 1 and -1 give their power, 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and other bases raise `IntegerOverflow`. For a result that is not an integer, write `2.0^(-1)`, or a `QQ` base as `(2/3)^(-1)`, not `10^(-k)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has integer powers only at `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `NN64`, each with an exponent of its own type; its `RR64` power takes an `RR64` or a `ZZ32` exponent, a negative one included.     98	
    99	**`/` on two integers answers a `QQ`.** So `7 / 2` is `7/2`, not 3. Truncate with `DIV`, on both paths. `DIV` answers its operands' type and rounds toward zero. For a float, make one operand a float, as `(1.0 s) / n` for `ZZ32` values `s` and `n`. Convert each `ZZ64` operand with `asFloat`, as `asFloat(s) / asFloat(n)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has no `QQ` and declares `/` only at `RR64`, so a compiled `7 / 2` is a static error.
   100	
   101	## Reductions and comprehensions
   102	
   103	A clause form is a reduction or comprehension with generators in brackets, as `SUM[j <- 0#n] f(j)`.
   104	
   105	**A reduction's static argument depends on the path.** The checker does not infer it for `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MAX` and `BIG MIN`, whose bound names the parameter (row 731). Write it in every clause form, as `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. Other reductions take their bound, or the expected type where the bound does not fit. Walk instantiates a reduction at its value's declared type: a local variable's, or a top-level or local function's return type, also where the clause form ends a block. A method's return type, a field, a top-level variable, a parameter and an assignment do not direct it. Else walk takes the join of the elements' run-time types.    107	- with no declared type, an empty `SUM` gives the integer 0 (row 716);

   110

   114	
   115	**Walk has no static types.** Walk will run the checker only after the switch-over (P-12). So walk runs programs that the checker refuses. content.content:
## A small change to the existing process

Replace the post-landing update instruction with a rule of this form:

> After a landing, update the skill where the landed tree changes what a worker must understand or do. Rewrite the existing explanation of that subject. State the current rule, its scope and the exceptions needed to use it. Keep a short contrast with the original Fortress only when it prevents a likely mistake. Put the repair history and supporting evidence in sources and reports. A landing does not require a new Revival entry.

Use the same intent in the writer's brief and Revival's introduction. Otherwise the old “each change” instruction remains a competing requirement. This is a proposed change of policy for approval, not a wording correction already applied.

Within the existing writer task:

1. Identify the current guidance affected by the landed findings. Decide whether to replace it, add a necessary qualification, link to its existing home, or make no skill change.
2. State the resulting rule without the batch narrative. Preserve path and library differences. An unresolved gap is current information when it changes how a worker must act.
3. Update sources for each changed rule. Use the guidance heading and exact evidence location. Keep the maintained text understandable without that evidence file.
4. Check nearby guidance and other entries that state the same behaviour. Do this by bounded search, not a whole-corpus rewrite.

In the existing cold read, add two questions:

> What would you do differently after reading this section? State the rule and its limits without opening the sources.

> Does this section contain repair history or detail that changes no action and prevents no misunderstanding?

The writer's evidence check remains separate. Retain the existing consolidation question:

> **Does this summary let a reader conclude more than the evidence establishes?**

Do not turn “no search” into “include every detail”. A worker should not need sources to understand the skill's rule. It can still follow a clear link to another skill part or a detailed report when its task requires that detail.

### Consolidation procedure

This is a one-time consolidation followed by the smaller update rule above. Do not shorten each of the 54 entries independently: that preserves the wrong unit of organization.

1. **Set the reading contract.** Revival is the short account of current departures from the original Fortress that workers must know before work. Core skill definitions may be assumed. Batch history and the coordinator's full record may not be assumed.
2. **Choose a provisional budget.** Aim for 8–12 thousand characters, near the original scale. This is a proposed editorial target, not a known tool limit or a reason to omit necessary qualifications. Verify that the complete file can be returned without truncation by the actual worker reading tool. Also judge its cost alongside the core skill.
3. **Draft a current-state outline.** Start with the existing language topics: dispatch, traits, static parameters and sizes, numerics, generators and reductions, and implementation limits. Organize by concepts workers use, not by repairs. Merge several repairs when together they establish one rule.
4. **Account for the old content in a temporary review table.** For each old entry, name its destination: retained current rule; merged rule; detail already in an area skill or report; history in sources; or unresolved discrepancy. This table is a review artifact, not another permanent registry. Check an actual destination before dropping unique information. If a useful fact exists only in the skill, flag it for the normal FACTS pass rather than silently discarding it.
5. **Write from the outline.** Give the current rule, the scope and exceptions required to apply it, and at most a short contrast or example where it prevents a likely error. Link to the relevant area skill for specialist detail. Keep essential path differences in the orientation itself. Do not require sources to understand a rule.
6. **Check preservation and comprehension separately.** Compare the draft against the source-backed old rules and the disposition table. Then cold-read the whole draft with the core skill, without the old Revival or batch reports. Ask a few concrete questions about the distinctions that must survive, including walk versus compiled behaviour and numeric result types. A shorter file that produces wrong answers fails.
7. **Publish the consolidation with its provenance.** Update sources so a maintainer can trace each new heading to the old entries and supporting evidence. Keep historical source entries; add a mapping for renamed or merged headings. Update the core skill's description and the post-landing instruction together. Thereafter replace affected explanations rather than append repair narratives.

Retain the one-entry trial as calibration, then consolidate the whole orientation to this outline. Merely demonstrating a shorter integer-power entry does not solve the 74K-file problem.

### Acceptance and maintenance

The consolidation is done when the file can be read whole, the scope distinctions survive, no unique finding is lost without a destination, and a cold reader can state how to work differently. Report the before/after character counts and any remaining size exception. If the target cannot be met without losing essential meaning, expose that conflict instead of compressing the prose into unexplained shorthand.

For each later landing, continue to record established findings in FACTS and gaps in the ledger, with their existing histories. Then ask which of those findings changes the small worker orientation. Many will change only a specialist skill part or no skill text at all. New content must compete for space through consolidation; it must not bypass the budget merely because it is new.

<!-- Seven principles by which the fortress-repo skill is written as the curator would write it, each with its reason and a pair of texts from the skill's history, the one he marked and the one he accepted, for the writer of its parts. -->

# Writing the skills

The curator directs this restoration and reads every skill with human eyes. The writer edits a skill, a part is a file under its `references/`, and the record is the project's memory under `explorations/`. The register is Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100), about halfway. Each principle gives its reason, then a text he marked and the text he accepted.

## 1. Define a term before you use it, and use plain words everywhere else

A reader new to the repository has only the skill, its brief and its training. A word with a meaning that the record gave it (a defect's "home", a "stop" that does not stop, "corpus") tells it nothing or the wrong thing. Where its training holds a near thing, name it ("as LLVM's lit does"): one clause corrects an assumption where a paragraph would not.
- Marked: "In every report, give each defect's home, ..."
- Accepted: "In your report, list each defect that you found, with the test or ledger row that records it."

## 2. Put the concepts first, as a dictionary, then the procedures in the order that the work meets them

A chain of do's and don'ts cannot be held in mind; a concept named once (an area, building, exploring, a point to report) makes each procedure short and tells the reader when to switch. A glossary entry is the term, then a noun phrase with no article. A comment marks a problem area: fix it at its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
- Marked: "- The base is the commit that your work starts from."
- Accepted: "**base**" / ": Commit that your work starts from."

## 3. Every sentence tells the reader what to do or a fact it needs to do it; cut the rest

Every agent pays for every token, and a sentence that changes nothing hides the ones that do: a slogan (a decision's title copied from the record), a step the agent takes anyway, a rule it cannot act on, a rule against a failure that never happened, a rule its system prompt gives, a back reference, a provenance word.
- Marked: "1. Read your brief. 2. Load the parts below that your task touches. [...] 4. Do the work."
- Accepted: "Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words [...]"

## 4. State a rule for exactly the cases where it holds, and bound it to the agent's brief and its own work

A wider rule sends the agent to do what cannot be done: a test for a specification edit, a search through other agents' transcripts, a question to the curator. An absolute ("never wipe the caches") is wrong in the cases it did not name. Authority reaches an agent through its brief alone, and what a role or a workflow does belongs there, not in the skill.
- Marked: "Before you build or run something, look for its result on record. If the record or another agent's transcript holds the result [...], cite that result"
- Accepted: "Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate or a test that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it."

Misapplied: cutting the default for a silent brief ("If it says nothing, commit your own files as you go") leaves the agent with no action. A cut never removes a default.

## 5. Say what to do, in the positive, one instruction per sentence, the condition first; add a reason only where it helps judge a case the rule does not name

A prohibition hides the mechanism it protects ("Do not ask the curator anything" hid how a question reaches him), and a compressed rule loses its purpose. A sentence that carries a list, a quoted title and a pointer cannot be held in mind; three short ones can.
- Marked: "Change one variable per step."
- Accepted: "When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause."

## 6. State a fact once, where the reader builds on it, and never in more words than the text you replace

The curator reads for duplication at every scale: a word written twice, a fact said twice, a paragraph where a sentence does. A longer rewrite is a regression, however clear.
- Marked: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: `tail` prints only after the command ends, and only its last lines. If the Bash tool's time limit stops the run first, you see nothing [...]"
- Accepted: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing."

Misapplied: a word repeated for two things (the `walk` command walks the tree) is not duplication; the rule is one word for one thing, and a pronoun for the second mention of the same thing.

## 7. Put knowledge in the part loaded when it is needed; name a note only with a trigger and a narrow read

A mention of a file does not make an agent open it at the right moment, and a large note read whole costs more than the task. So the part holds what daily work needs, and a note it names comes with when to open it and the query that prints the slice. What only the coordinating session needs stays out of a skill every worker loads.
- Marked: "`explorations/modernization-plan.md` gives the versions and the classfile level."
- Accepted: "Before you change the version of a tool, read its step in the modernization plan. [...] It prints 4 to 6 KB: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/modernization-plan.md#The ladder@TOOL'`."

(* An expression of numerals alone folds exactly into a numeral before walk runs it: integer arithmetic past ZZ32, a negative numeral, a p40, a decimal tenths, a quotient, CHOOSE outside its range, and two natural numerals concatenated; constant.tex, section "Types of Static Expressions". *)
component NumeralFoldWalk
export Executable

isZZ32(x: Any): Boolean = typecase x of
    ZZ32 => true
    else => false
  end

isZZ64(x: Any): Boolean = typecase x of
    ZZ64 => true
    else => false
  end

isQQ(x: Any): Boolean = typecase x of
    QQ => true
    else => false
  end

run():() = do
  over = 2147483647 + 1
  assert(isZZ64(over), "2147483647 + 1 folds into a numeral that takes ZZ64")
  assert(over = 2147483648, "2147483647 + 1 is 2147483648")
  least = -2147483648
  assert(isZZ32(least), "-2147483648 folds into a numeral that fits ZZ32")
  p40 = 2^40
  assert(p40 = 1099511627776, "2^40 is 1099511627776")
  jx = 65536 65536
  assert(jx = 4294967296, "65536 65536 is 4294967296")
  dt = 65536 DOT 65536
  assert(dt = 4294967296, "65536 DOT 65536 is 4294967296")
  tenths = 0.1 + 0.2
  assert(tenths = 0.3, "0.1 + 0.2 folds into the numeral 0.3")
  q72 = 7/2
  assert(isQQ(q72), "7/2 is a QQ")
  assert(q72 = 7/2, "7/2 keeps its value")
  c35 = 3 CHOOSE 5
  assert(c35, 0, "3 CHOOSE 5 is 0; basic-integers.tex, section \"Integers\", opr CHOOSE")
  cneg = 5 CHOOSE (-1)
  assert(cneg, 0, "5 CHOOSE (-1) is 0")
  c103 = 10 CHOOSE 3
  assert(c103, 120, "10 CHOOSE 3 is 120")
  hexWord = deadc_16 || 0de_16
  assert(hexWord, deadc0de_16, "deadc_16 || 0de_16 is deadc0de_16; constant.tex, section \"Types of Static Expressions\"")
  q16 = (1/3) + (1/6)
  assert(q16 = 1/2, "(1/3) + (1/6) is 1/2")
  qneg = (-7) / 2
  assert(isQQ(qneg), "(-7) / 2 is a QQ")
  diff = 0.1 - 0.3
  assert(diff = -0.2, "0.1 - 0.3 folds into prefix minus on the numeral 0.2")
  tiny = 10.0^(-5)
  assert(tiny = 0.00001, "10.0^(-5) folds into the numeral 0.00001")
  assert(0.3 = 0.1 + 0.2, "0.3 = 0.1 + 0.2 folds exactly")
  dz = try
      1 DIV 0
    catch e
      DivisionByZero => -7
    end
  assert(dz, -7, "1 DIV 0 is left to raise DivisionByZero")
end
a coercion from \TYP{NaturalNumeral}, and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}
and \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} declare one from \TYP{RadixPointNumeral}; the conversion
is exact into the five integer types (\secref{basic-integers}) and
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, and rounds once, to the nearest value of the type, into
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}32}.

A place \emph{fixes a type} for a numeral when the type declared there declares
a coercion from the numeral's type, as each number type of \library\ does and a
type of a program's own may, or is a numeral type itself.
The declared type of a variable, a field or a parameter, and the declared
return type of a functional, are such places, the parameter types of the
declaration that a call invokes among them (\secref{resolving-coercion}).
There the numeral is converted into that type, from its exact value:
so \EXP{q\COLON\mathbb{Q} = 0.1} binds the rational \EXP{1/10},
\EXP{r\COLON\mathbb{R}64 = 0.1} the floating-point number nearest to it, and
\EXP{n\COLON\mathbb{N}32 = 5} the natural number 5.
It is a static error if the numeral's value lies outside the range of that
type, or rounds to an infinity there.
Where nothing fixes a type, as where a variable is declared without a type, or
a parameter has the type \TYP{Any}, \TYP{Object} or \TYP{Number} or a type
parameter declared without a bound, the numeral is converted into its
\emph{default}: a numeral without a radix point into \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or into
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its value does not fit in the
narrower type, and a numeral with a radix point into \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
So \EXP{x = 3} binds \VAR{x} as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32},
\EXP{\VAR{bigN} = 3000000000} binds \VAR{bigN} as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} and
\EXP{y = 0.5} binds \VAR{y} as an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64};
\EXP{x \sequiv z} is \VAR{true} for \EXP{z\COLON\mathbb{Z}32 = 3};
and for \EXP{\KWD{object}\;\TYP{Cell}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)},
\EXP{\TYP{Cell}(3)} is a \EXP{\TYP{Cell}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}32\rrbracket}.
\secref{numeral-default} says where else a numeral takes its default, as where
several numerals fix one type parameter, and how a numeral whose conversions
tie is read.
The default applies to a numeral, and to a static expression of numerals once
it is folded (\secref{static-expr}), never to an expression of a numeral type.

A type of a program's own receives a numeral through its own coercion from the
numeral's type, such as \EXP{\KWD{coerce}(x\COLON\TYP{RadixPointNumeral})},
whose body reads the four numbers.
A numeral at a place whose type is a type of a program's own that declares no
coercion from the numeral's type is a static error: coercion does not chain
(\secref{coercion}), so the numeral is not converted into its default first.

38:- P-40 **Sizes are checked, and a size that inference leaves unknown is an error only where it is used.** A size is a `nat` or `int` static parameter, such as the length of an array in its type. The compiled checker checks sizes, and refuses a size beyond `NN32` or `ZZ32` (F-140, the bound on both paths). Wherever the array design, the compiled path's design for arrays (P-85), creates a JVM array, it checks the length there, at run time, and refuses one over 2^31-1. A size that inference leaves unknown is an error only when it reaches a type, a name or a value. So a declaration may declare a size that none of its types uses, and pass. A call that cannot fix a size of the declaration that it would choose is refused, also inside an overload set, instead of passing over that declaration. In the rule that no type extends two different instantiations of one generic trait, two instantiations differ when any static argument but an operator differs, so `Vec[\3\]` and `Vec[\4\]` are two; boolean arguments count too once the checker has boolean parameters. A size used as a number, as in the range `0#n`, converts to `ZZ32` where one is needed, as a numeral does. The 17 vector and matrix operators of the `FortressLibrary` api declare only the sizes that their types use, the change of `explorations/perf-probes/array-sites/e3-rebased.patch`. It finishes the team's own fix of 2008, which removed those sizes from the component only. The JVM length check waits for the array design; under walk such an array stops at its store's factory with walk's own error, which no catch sees (row 527). The checker still passes over a declaration whose unfixed size occurs in its own parameter type (row 400). The checker compares no boolean arguments (row 406).
76:- P-169 **The runtime's own 13 native bindings, the arrays' store, threads with `abort` and the task trace, name compiled helpers that walk's loader answers with walk's own operations, P-167's device, in two compiled shapes.** Each keeps P-58's form, a bare `builtinPrimitive("…")` naming a helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the compiled path runs; walk's loader answers the name with walk's glue, so walk keeps its `AtomicArray` store and its `spawn`, and for these names P-58's walk half bends, as for P-167's two. The arrays' 7, of `PrimitiveArray`, `PrimImmutableArray` and `PrimImmutableRR64Array`: the compiled half by P-164's device, a store trait in `FortressLibrary` whose bindings name helpers of a new `nativeHelpers/arrayOps` over a compiled class that holds the elements; `PrimitiveArray` and `PrimImmutableArray` leave the native component and hold the store in a field, and walk's native object below the trait holds an `AtomicArray`; `PrimImmutableRR64Array`'s two are on a compiled `double[]` class that no factory chooses until array decision A (P-84, P-85; F-333). The compiled store is an `Object[]`, and the compiled transaction tracks its reads and writes by the array and the index (`TXReadSlot`, `TXWriteSlot`): P-84 stores every number type's array unboxed, so a compiled `atomic` write into any array needs that keying, and an array of objects keeps one box an element, not two. Threads, `abort` and the task trace, 6: helpers in a `nativeHelpers` class over the compiled runtime, as the team's `nativeHelpers/runtime.java` is (F-335); `Thread`'s `val`, `wait`, `ready` and `stop` raise until the code generator compiles `spawn` (row 82). +# What the revival changed in the team's Fortress
+
+This part gives the departures of revived Fortress from the team's Fortress, and from what you expect from Java, Scala, Haskell or Julia. The team left three forms that disagree: the specification, walk with the interpreter's library, and the compiled path with the compiler's library. The rules below resolve them. Read the part whole, after `SKILL.md`, before work.
+
+Each bold rule states the rule of this tree. A sentence that names a POSITIONS entry (P-N) states a decision of the curator. Build on a sentence without one, but do not cite it as a decision. Question a rule only on new evidence (`SKILL.md`, "When to explore"). Most rules follow the team's later type papers (`Papers/`) over the specification's early text (P-26; `exploring.md`). The Working Draft is the unrevised specification, in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`. Where a rule changed the specification, Appendix I keeps the original text (`specification.md`).
+
+A sentence that cites a ledger row states a known departure of one path from a bold rule. A fix can change it, so do not assert it as correct in a test. A sentence that opens "Until the switch-over" states a limit of the compiler's library. The limit ends when the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library, so do not fix it in the compiler's prelude (`compiler.md`). If a change is not here, search FACTS and POSITIONS (`records.md`) before you call a disagreement a conflict. An old note, a team test and your training can be right about the team's walk and wrong here: the number types do not nest, fixed-width arithmetic does not wrap, and walk converts arguments.
+
+## Dispatch and overloading
+
+**Overloads may differ in their static parameters (P-45).** An example is `ident[\T extends Shape\](x: T): T` beside `ident[\T extends Round\](x: T): T`. The Working Draft forbids such pairs. A declaration's declared domain is the set of argument types that its declared parameter types accept at some instance within its bounds: every `Shape` for the first `ident`. The checker applies the overloading rules of `SKILL.md` to declared domains. The more specific declaration's return type must be a subtype of the other's at every instance, not at one only.
+
+**Where a declaration has static parameters, exclusion is read over the whole tuple of parameter types (P-152).** By the exclusion rule, a value of both domains has one instance of each generic type at each position, so those instances' static arguments are equal. The domains exclude where these equalities cannot hold together, or where some position excludes at the instance that they force. So `o[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: Box[\T\])` beside `o[\T\](x: Q[\T\], b: Box[\T\])`, with `P[\T\] excludes { Q[\T\] }`, is valid. Both paths refuse a pair where the equalities leave a static parameter free, as `o[\T, U\](x: Q[\U\], b: Box[\T\])` beside the first `o`: nothing ties `U` to `T`. In its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays.
+
+**Walk chooses by declared parameter types, never by the order of the declarations.** It compares declared domains where one lies strictly inside the other. Otherwise it compares the instances that the call makes. It infers a dotted generic method's static arguments from the arguments' run-time types, as for a generic function. A trait's generic method called with an argument outside a bound fails with "Cannot unify".
+
+**Walk's load check is not the verdict of these rules.** It refuses some valid pairs and loads some invalid ones, and the checker differs from it on others. Before you change code to pass walk's check, or take its acceptance as proof, find the case in `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks": a case that cites a ledger row is a departure of walk. For example, walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their declared domains only at a call (row 780).
+
+**Two functional methods with equivalent parameter types are duplicates, wherever `self` stands.** So the checker refuses `f(self, y: S)` beside `f(x: S, self)` in a trait `S`. Abstract declarations count:
+
+- both paths refuse an abstract and a concrete method with the same parameter types in one trait;
+- both paths refuse an object that inherits an abstract functional method from one trait and its body from another, unless the object declares the method itself (P-149). The Scala language accepts it.
+
+The Meet Rule asks for a declaration that covers the meet of two overloads that neither exclude each other nor nest (`SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language"). An abstract functional method also counts for it. So the checker refuses `h(self): ZZ32` in a trait `S` beside a top-level `h(x: String): ZZ32`: nothing covers the meet of `S` and `String`. Likewise, a program's trait that declares its own functional `+` overlaps the library's `+` between an array and a number, because a type can extend both the trait and `Number`, which has no `comprises` clause (P-160). Declare the trait `excludes { Number }`, or make it exclude arrays, `excludes { HasRank }`. Or declare the `+` in an object, not in a trait: an object excludes every trait that it does not extend, because no other type can extend it. Otherwise walk refuses the program at load: "fails the Meet Rule". The checker refuses such a pair in one component, but accepts it against the library's `+` (row 918). Give a trait with its own functional `-`, `MIN` or `MAX` the same fix: the library declares these in the same form.
+
+## Traits and objects
+
+**The compiled checker applies the exclusion rule (P-43, P-97).** It refuses a type that extends two instantiations of one generic trait. Walk does not apply the rule: it runs such a type, and refuses overloads on two instantiations, as `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])`, because it does not read them as excluding (row 416). The specification marks the Working Draft's examples that break the rule "Not allowed": do not copy them.
+
+**A `comprises` clause speaks of values (P-60).** Every value of the trait that declares it is a value of a listed type. So a generic trait need not be listed if every type below it is below a listed type, as `Integral[\I\]` below `AnyIntegral`. A Java `permits` list names each direct subtype; this clause need not. Read so, several declarations can together cover the meet of two overloads. At load, walk checks extenders only against the clauses of the program's main component (row 551).
+
+**`override` widens.** An `override` overrides an inherited declaration only where the inherited parameter types are strictly narrower than its own. To replace an inherited declaration at its own parameter types, declare it again without `override`. An `override` in a trait also overrides in every type below it. The checker checks that an overriding return type is a subtype. Walk refuses at load an `override` that, by this rule, overrides nothing, so a Java-style `override` in the library stops every program. Two departures: the checker accepts such an `override` (row 653), and the code generator refuses every `override` modifier (row 650).
+
+**An object defines an inherited abstract method by bodies that together cover its parameter types (P-147).** It needs one body at those types, or several narrower bodies that cover them, with `comprises` clauses read. Walk refuses at load an object without static parameters that leaves one uncovered. Walk skips this check for a generic object (row 665). Walk stops its search for a cover at limits that `interpreter.md` gives, and the checker at the same limits. The checker refuses a cover by several bodies where the abstract or a covering method has static parameters (row 725).
+
+**In a self-typed trait the checker types `self` as the trait met with the implementing type.** A trait `T` is self-typed if both conditions hold:
+
+- `T` has no `comprises` clause, or one that lists only `...`;
+- `T` has a parameter `X` bounded by `T` itself, as `trait T[\X extends T[\X\]\]` (P-146), or by a self-typed trait `U[\X\]` that `T` extends, as `trait T[\X extends U[\X\]\] extends U[\X\]`.
+
+In `T`'s bodies, `self` has the intersection type of `T[\X\]` and `X`. So `floor(self): I = self` in `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]` is valid without a cast. The checker refuses a type that extends `T[\A\]` and is not an `A`. A compiled body of `T` that returns `self` fails the JVM's verification when its class loads (row 695).
+
+When the checker applies the overloading rules to a method of `T`, `self` has the type `T[\X\]`, except in its test of whether two domains exclude each other. There `self` has the intersection type of `T[\X\]` and `X` (P-157). With this reading and the bounds that the test reads ("Dispatch and overloading"), the library's generic `+` and `-` between an array and a number are valid beside `AdditiveGroup`'s own. Walk reads `self` in the same way, so it loads such a pair in the library and in a program's own component. Walk's load check, which is not the verdict ("Dispatch and overloading"), still refuses the pair in two cases:
+
+- `T` is self-typed only through another self-typed trait that it extends;
+- `T`'s method has static parameters of its own.
+
+**An indexed type's index parameter is bounded by `Index` (P-156).** An indexed type is a type whose values `a[i]` subscripts, such as an array. Its index parameter is the static parameter that gives the type of `i`. In the library, and in your own generic over such a type, write `I extends Index`. Walk runs the code without the bound. The checker refuses it when it checks against the interpreter's library, as the count stage does (`compiler.md`). Of the integer types, only `ZZ32` extends `Index`, and `Range` excludes `Index`. A numeral there takes its default, a `ZZ32`, so `f(3)` is valid for `f(x: Index)`. The Working Draft lets no trait type hold a tuple, but here a tuple whose element types are all `Index` types is an `Index`. So `m[i, j]` passes the pair `(i, j)` as one index. `Index` extends only `Any`, so such a tuple is still no `Object`. The empty tuple `()` is no `Index`. A function over `Index` and one over a tuple of `Index` types do not exclude each other. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude declares no `Index`, so a program that names it does not compile: write the bound only in code that runs under walk or is checked against the interpreter's library. Two departures:
+
+- the checker refuses a tuple expression at a parameter of type `Index`, but takes one at a parameter of type `I`, where `I extends Index` (row 805);
+- walk loads a function over `Index` beside one over a pair whose element types neither lie below `Index` nor exclude it (row 806).
+
+**Pairs and triples are ordered only where each element type extends `StandardPartialOrder`.** This holds for `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` and `CMP`. Walk refuses another element type at the call, also where earlier elements decide, as `(1,()) < (2,())`. It also refuses numbers of two run-time types at one position, as `(1,2) < (1,2.5)` (row 511). Unordered deciding elements give `false`, or `Unordered` for `CMP`. The checker orders a `List[\E\]` only where `E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\]`, so a list of `RR64` has no order there (P-154). Walk orders every list (row 774). A list's `=` stays element by element.
+
+**Where a type declares no `=`, `=` is strict equivalence, `SEQV` (P-168).** Strict equivalence is the operator `≣` (STRICTLY EQUIVALENT TO), written `SEQV` or `===` in ASCII. The operator `≡` (IDENTICAL TO, `EQV` or `EQUIV`) is a different one: logical equivalence on booleans. The interpreter's library declares it for no type, and walk stops on it (row 184): write `a <-> b`. The library's `=` over `Any` answers `a SEQV b`. `SEQV` follows the specification on both paths:
+
+- values of different types are never equivalent;
+- a value object is equivalent field by field, a tuple element by element, an integer, a character or a boolean by its value, and a float by its bits;
+- a reference object, a string among them, is equivalent only to itself;
+- a function is equivalent to itself, but may be found unequal to another that behaves the same.
+
+So for a value object `V` without its own `=`, `V(s) = V(t)` is `false` where `s` and `t` are equal strings made by two computations. Two string literals of one text are one object (P-171). So `"ab" SEQV "ab"` and `V("ab") = V("ab")` are `true`. Two string literals joined by `||` fold into one literal, so `("a" || "b") SEQV "ab"` is `true` (P-171; the Working Draft, `constant.tex:75-79`). A float numeral converts where `RR64` is declared ("Numbers"), so `y: RR64 = 0.5` is `SEQV` a computed `x: RR64 = 0.25 + 0.25`. Walk departs from both answers (rows 943, 945), and the compiled path from the string answer (row 945); `interpreter.md` and `compiler.md` give the departures. The interpreter's library declares `=` on pairs and triples only, so `(s, 1, 2, 3) = (t, 1, 2, 3)` falls back to `SEQV` and is `false`; row 923 holds the question of longer tuples. Its own `≣`, declared as `===`, compares strings and `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `RR32` and `RR64` by `=`, not by bits or identity (row 908).
+
+## Static parameters, `where` clauses and sizes
+
+**A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound, not Scala's `Nothing` (P-48).** The checker takes the intersection of its upper bounds, narrowed by the expected type. Under walk, a parameter whose bound names itself stays open, printed `OPEN`, as in `BoxU[\OPEN\]`. Every value passes `OPEN` itself. Where walk compares overloads, a type that holds `OPEN` admits only what it admits at `Bottom`: beside `pick(x: Any)`, `pick(x: (T,T))` takes no `(1, 2)`. Walk still gives `Bottom` to these parameters:
+
+- one with two bounds, neither below the other (row 591);
+- one that an argument bounds only from above, with a bound that names another static parameter (row 612);
+- one that only the result of a function expression without a return type fixes (row 587).
+
+**Only the checker gives a call written as an argument the enclosing call's context (P-51).** If the enclosing call fails as written, the checker types the inner call again against each declaration's parameter type. So `takesBox64(mk())` compiles for `mk[\T\](): BoxT[\T\]`. Walk gives an argument no expected type, so there `mk()` takes its bound (row 705). Under walk, write `mk[\ZZ64\]()`.
+
+**Three `where` forms are built (P-151).** Conditional extension is an `extends` entry with a `where` clause that binds no variable and states only constraints `T extends SomeTrait`. The type extends the parent only where they hold, as `List[\E\]` extends `LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\] where { E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\] }`. The other two forms:
+
+- a condition of a function or method on its own static parameters, or of a method on its trait's, checked at a call;
+- a type variable of a `where` clause in a `comprises` clause, as `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`.
+
+The checker reads an `extends` entry with any other `where` clause as unconditional, without a message. Walk and the compiled runtime apply a conditional extension at every instance (row 774). Walk runs a dotted call that breaks a method's condition (row 777). The code generator accepts a declaration's own `where` clause but emits no code for it, so the compiled runtime does not check it. A compiled call of a function or method whose own clause introduces a `where`-clause variable, as `where [\nat n\]` does, dies at run time (row 867). `compiler.md` gives the checker's gaps.
+
+**Sizes are compared by their written form (P-55).** The checker checks sizes against their kind, and the runtime carries each as a descriptor. Two sizes are equal when they are written alike after numeral arithmetic: `2 3` is `6`, but `s0 s1` is not `s1 s0`. A static parameter is not known to differ from a numeral, so in `typecase N[\b0\] of N[\0\] => ...` the arm is reachable. The checker refuses a size power above the exponent 4096, except of 0, 1 or -1. Walk refuses a negative exponent. The class loader computes a size without checking its kind, and stops on a negative exponent with a Java exception (row 675).
+
+**A size known only at run time comes from `reflect` in `NatReflect.fsi`.** Its value, a `NatParam`, passed where the object type `N[\n\]` is expected, binds `n` at the call. Such a call does not run compiled yet. Until the switch-over, compiled programs do not link `NatReflect`, which is part of the interpreter's library. After the switch-over, such a call still fails, for a second reason. `NatParam` is declared `comprises { N[\n\] } where [\nat n\]`, so its `comprises` clause lists a type at a `where`-clause size. A compiled call fails the JVM's verification if it passes a value of such a trait where a listed type is expected (row 307). This holds for a program's own trait too.
+
+## Numbers
+
+**The number types are flat siblings (P-43).** The record calls this choice route A. Route C is the way not chosen: a checker rule under which the number types could nest again. The record still calls the number and order traits "the tower". That word does not mean that they nest.
+
+**A numeral has a type of its own, which holds its exact value (P-76, P-172).** The checker types an integer numeral as `IntLiteral`, a sibling under `Number` that converts to the integer types, `QQ` and `RR64`. Under walk, the specification's revised text gives an integer numeral the type `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` where its value does not fit, until walk runs the checker (`Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:159-165`). Walk today builds a generic from it at its own class instead (row 364; `interpreter.md`). A numeral with a radix point is a `FloatLiteral`. `QQ` converts from it exactly, and `RR64` and `RR32` with one rounding, so `1/2 = 0.5` is `true`. The library's factories `array1` and `array2` give a `Vector` or a `Matrix` only at the eight number types; at a program's own number type they give a plain array. `interpreter.md`, "How walk evaluates a program", lists where walk departs from these rules (rows 364, 721, 943, 944).
+
+**Arguments convert by declared coercions, and a generic call promotes.** Walk converts at a call, a typed binding and an assignment, and chooses the coercion by the run-time value; the checker chooses it statically (P-59). Promotion instantiates a generic declaration at the narrowest type into which all its arguments coerce (P-74). So `f[\T\](a: T, b: T)` on a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` runs at `ZZ64`. Walk does not promote the elements of a tuple or varargs: it takes their join (rows 395, 511). Where several declarations apply only by coercion and none is more specific, both paths stop: "Ambiguous coercion". Where the tied declarations differ only at the positions of the call's numerals, the checker reads the numeral as `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` where the value does not fit.
+
+**An integer converts to another integer type by a checked getter or by a low-bits function (P-161).** To convert a value, write a getter, as `x.asZZ32`: `asZZ32`, `asZZ64`, `asNN32`, `asNN64` or `asZZ`. It keeps the value or raises `IntegerOverflow`. The low-bits functions `narrow`, `widen`, `signed`, `unsigned` and `big` keep the low bits and never raise, as Java's `(int)` does. On the fixed-width types, `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32` and `NN64`, `narrow` and `widen` give the 32-bit and the 64-bit type of the same sign, `signed` and `unsigned` the signed and the unsigned type of the same width, and `big` a `ZZ`. So `narrow` of a `ZZ64` outside `ZZ32`'s range wraps silently. In the interpreter's library, each fixed-width type has all five functions, and one that keeps the type returns the value, as `widen` of a `ZZ64`. `ZZ` has only `big`, so for a `ZZ` value `z`, `narrow(z)` finds no declaration: write `z.asZZ32`. Each `bitsAs…` getter equals `unsigned` or `signed`, as `bitsAsNN32` of a `ZZ32`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude has only these getters: `asZZ` on each fixed-width type, `asZZ32` on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`, `asNN32` on `NN32`, and `asNN64` on `NN64`. It has no `big`, and of the low-bits functions only those that change the type, as `narrow` of a `ZZ64` (row 349).
+
+**`Number` declares nothing (P-165).** Each of the eight number types, and `IntLiteral`, declares its own `asFloat` into `RR64`. So generic code over `T extends Number` can call on a `T` no method or operator that the number types declare, `asFloat` among them. Two numbers of different types compare by `=` only where a coercion carries one into the other: the library declares `=` for each such pair, so a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` of equal value are `=`. Otherwise `=` is `SEQV` ("Traits and objects"), and answers `false` without an error, as for a `ZZ64` against an equal `RR64`. To compare values across types at known types, write `asFloat(x) = y`. In generic code over `T extends Number`, declare your function once for each number type instead. A program may also declare its own number type below `Number` (P-160).
+
+**An integer power answers its base's type (P-153).** In the interpreter's library, `^` takes an exponent of any integer type. At a negative exponent, 1 and -1 give their power, 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and other bases raise `IntegerOverflow`. For a result that is not an integer, write `2.0^(-1)`, or a `QQ` base as `(2/3)^(-1)`, not `10^(-k)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has integer powers only at `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `NN64`, each with an exponent of its own type; its `RR64` power takes an `RR64` or a `ZZ32` exponent, a negative one included. Its `ZZ32` power gives 0 at a negative exponent for other bases. At a base of 0 it throws a Java exception that no `catch` sees (rows 441, 523).
+
+**`/` on two integers answers a `QQ`.** So `7 / 2` is `7/2`, not 3. Truncate with `DIV`, on both paths. `DIV` answers its operands' type and rounds toward zero. For a float, make one operand a float, as `(1.0 s) / n` for `ZZ32` values `s` and `n`. Convert each `ZZ64` operand with `asFloat`, as `asFloat(s) / asFloat(n)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has no `QQ` and declares `/` only at `RR64`, so a compiled `7 / 2` is a static error.
+
+## Reductions and comprehensions
+
+A clause form is a reduction or comprehension with generators in brackets, as `SUM[j <- 0#n] f(j)`.
+
+**A reduction's static argument depends on the path.** The checker does not infer it for `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MAX` and `BIG MIN`, whose bound names the parameter (row 731). Write it in every clause form, as `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. Other reductions take their bound, or the expected type where the bound does not fit. Walk instantiates a reduction at its value's declared type: a local variable's, or a top-level or local function's return type, also where the clause form ends a block. A method's return type, a field, a top-level variable, a parameter and an assignment do not direct it. Else walk takes the join of the elements' run-time types. If that join is outside the reduction's bound, each `+` runs at its operands' types. An element that does not convert to the instance stops in `__bigOperator`, "body param 1". Departures under walk:
+
+- with no declared type, an empty `SUM` gives the integer 0 (row 716);
+- a comprehension inside another clause form is built at its elements' run-time types (rows 20, 717);
+- a written static argument that is not a number type ends an empty `SUM` in `CastError` (row 436).

+# What the revival changed in the team's Fortress
+
+This part gives the departures of revived Fortress from the team's Fortress, and from what you expect from Java, Scala, Haskell or Julia. The team left three forms that disagree: the specification, walk with the interpreter's library, and the compiled path with the compiler's library. The rules below resolve them. Read the part whole, after `SKILL.md`, before work.
+
+Each bold rule states the rule of this tree. A sentence that names a POSITIONS entry (P-N) states a decision of the curator. Build on a sentence without one, but do not cite it as a decision. Question a rule only on new evidence (`SKILL.md`, "When to explore"). Most rules follow the team's later type papers (`Papers/`) over the specification's early text (P-26; `exploring.md`). The Working Draft is the unrevised specification, in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`. Where a rule changed the specification, Appendix I keeps the original text (`specification.md`).
+
+A sentence that cites a ledger row states a known departure of one path from a bold rule. A fix can change it, so do not assert it as correct in a test. A sentence that opens "Until the switch-over" states a limit of the compiler's library. The limit ends when the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library, so do not fix it in the compiler's prelude (`compiler.md`). If a change is not here, search FACTS and POSITIONS (`records.md`) before you call a disagreement a conflict. An old note, a team test and your training can be right about the team's walk and wrong here: the number types do not nest, fixed-width arithmetic does not wrap, and walk converts arguments.
+
+## Dispatch and overloading
+
+**Overloads may differ in their static parameters (P-45).** An example is `ident[\T extends Shape\](x: T): T` beside `ident[\T extends Round\](x: T): T`. The Working Draft forbids such pairs. A declaration's declared domain is the set of argument types that its declared parameter types accept at some instance within its bounds: every `Shape` for the first `ident`. The checker applies the overloading rules of `SKILL.md` to declared domains. The more specific declaration's return type must be a subtype of the other's at every instance, not at one only.
+
+**Where a declaration has static parameters, exclusion is read over the whole tuple of parameter types (P-152).** By the exclusion rule, a value of both domains has one instance of each generic type at each position, so those instances' static arguments are equal. The domains exclude where these equalities cannot hold together, or where some position excludes at the instance that they force. So `o[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: Box[\T\])` beside `o[\T\](x: Q[\T\], b: Box[\T\])`, with `P[\T\] excludes { Q[\T\] }`, is valid. Both paths refuse a pair where the equalities leave a static parameter free, as `o[\T, U\](x: Q[\U\], b: Box[\T\])` beside the first `o`: nothing ties `U` to `T`. In its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays.
+
+**Walk chooses by declared parameter types, never by the order of the declarations.** It compares declared domains where one lies strictly inside the other. Otherwise it compares the instances that the call makes. It infers a dotted generic method's static arguments from the arguments' run-time types, as for a generic function. A trait's generic method called with an argument outside a bound fails with "Cannot unify".
+
+**Walk's load check is not the verdict of these rules.** It refuses some valid pairs and loads some invalid ones, and the checker differs from it on others. Before you change code to pass walk's check, or take its acceptance as proof, find the case in `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks": a case that cites a ledger row is a departure of walk. For example, walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object on their declared domains only at a call (row 780).
+
+**Two functional methods with equivalent parameter types are duplicates, wherever `self` stands.** So the checker refuses `f(self, y: S)` beside `f(x: S, self)` in a trait `S`. Abstract declarations count:
+
+- both paths refuse an abstract and a concrete method with the same parameter types in one trait;
+- both paths refuse an object that inherits an abstract functional method from one trait and its body from another, unless the object declares the method itself (P-149). The Scala language accepts it.
+
+The Meet Rule asks for a declaration that covers the meet of two overloads that neither exclude each other nor nest (`SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language"). An abstract functional method also counts for it. So the checker refuses `h(self): ZZ32` in a trait `S` beside a top-level `h(x: String): ZZ32`: nothing covers the meet of `S` and `String`. Likewise, a program's trait that declares its own functional `+` overlaps the library's `+` between an array and a number, because a type can extend both the trait and `Number`, which has no `comprises` clause (P-160). Declare the trait `excludes { Number }`, or make it exclude arrays, `excludes { HasRank }`. Or declare the `+` in an object, not in a trait: an object excludes every trait that it does not extend, because no other type can extend it. Otherwise walk refuses the program at load: "fails the Meet Rule". The checker refuses such a pair in one component, but accepts it against the library's `+` (row 918). Give a trait with its own functional `-`, `MIN` or `MAX` the same fix: the library declares these in the same form.
+
+## Traits and objects
+
+**The compiled checker applies the exclusion rule (P-43, P-97).** It refuses a type that extends two instantiations of one generic trait. Walk does not apply the rule: it runs such a type, and refuses overloads on two instantiations, as `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])`, because it does not read them as excluding (row 416). The specification marks the Working Draft's examples that break the rule "Not allowed": do not copy them.
+
+**A `comprises` clause speaks of values (P-60).** Every value of the trait that declares it is a value of a listed type. So a generic trait need not be listed if every type below it is below a listed type, as `Integral[\I\]` below `AnyIntegral`. A Java `permits` list names each direct subtype; this clause need not. Read so, several declarations can together cover the meet of two overloads. At load, walk checks extenders only against the clauses of the program's main component (row 551).
+
+**`override` widens.** An `override` overrides an inherited declaration only where the inherited parameter types are strictly narrower than its own. To replace an inherited declaration at its own parameter types, declare it again without `override`. An `override` in a trait also overrides in every type below it. The checker checks that an overriding return type is a subtype. Walk refuses at load an `override` that, by this rule, overrides nothing, so a Java-style `override` in the library stops every program. Where walk compares overloads, a type that holds `OPEN` admits only what it admits at `Bottom`: beside `pick(x: Any)`, `pick(x: (T,T))` takes no `(1, 2)`. Walk still gives `Bottom` to these parameters:
+
+- one with two bounds, neither below the other (row 591);
+- one that an argument bounds only from above, with a bound that names another static parameter (row 612);
+- one that only the result of a function expression without a return type fixes (row 587).
+

+
+- a condition of a function or method on its own static parameters, or of a method on its trait's, checked at a call;
+- a type variable of a `where` clause in a `comprises` clause, as `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`.
+

A compiled call of a function or method whose own clause introduces a `where`-clause variable, as `where [\nat n\]` does, dies at run time (row 867). `compiler.md` gives the checker's gaps.
+
+**Sizes are compared by their written form (P-55).** The checker checks sizes against their kind, and the runtime carries each as a descriptor. Two sizes are equal when they are written alike after numeral arithmetic: `2 3` is `6`, but `s0 s1` is not `s1 s0`. A static parameter is not known to differ from a numeral, so in `typecase N[\b0\] of N[\0\] => ...` the arm is reachable. The checker refuses a size power above the exponent 4096, except of 0, 1 or -1. Walk refuses a negative exponent. The class loader computes a size without checking its kind, and stops on a negative exponent with a Java exception (row 675).

After the switch-over, such a call still fails, for a second reason. `NatParam` is declared `comprises { N[\n\] } where [\nat n\]`, so its `comprises` clause lists a type at a `where`-clause size. +## Numbers
+
+**The number types are flat siblings (P-43).** The record calls this choice route A. Route C is the way not chosen: a checker rule under which the number types could nest again. The record still calls the number and order traits "the tower". That word does not mean that they nest.

A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as each of the eight number types has. Such places are a typed binding, an assignment, a field, a parameter and a declared return type. There the numeral converts from its exact value: exactly into the five integer types and `QQ`, and with one rounding into `RR64` and `RR32` (P-76, P-172). +## Reductions and comprehensions
+
+A clause form is a reduction or comprehension with generators in brackets, as `SUM[j <- 0#n] f(j)`.

+
+**Walk has no static types.** Walk will run the checker only after the switch-over (P-12). So walk runs programs that the checker refuses. +**Write every parameter type.** The compiled path refuses a parameter without a type, of a function, a method or a local function: "Missing parameter type for". Walk runs it, except in a method that implements an abstract one (row 405). A component's function that leaves out its return type takes the api's declaration at its parameter types.
